title: Adult Diaper Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A concentrated hygiene-products manufacturing niche supported by aging demographics, inelastic medical need and premium pull-up formats.
overview: The industry manufactures adult diapers, pull-ups, pads and other disposable incontinence products in the United States. Demand is unusually resilient because products are tied to chronic incontinence, aging, disability, post-surgical care and long-term care rather than discretionary spending. The 2022 IBIS baseline placed manufacturing revenue at $4.362 billion, and applying its 2022-2028 projected CAGR implies roughly $4.7 billion of US manufacturing revenue in 2025. Broader retail and healthcare demand is larger: current market sources put the 2025 US adult diaper market at about $6.43 billion, reflecting imports, wholesale/retail margins and adjacent products. The industry remains highly concentrated, capital intensive and brand driven, with Kimberly-Clark, Essity, First Quality, Attindas and institutional medical-supply channels shaping competition.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: approximately $4.7 billion in US manufacturing revenue, estimated from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline and 2022-2028 projected CAGR; broader 2025 US adult diaper market demand was estimated at $6.43 billion by IMARC.
key_stats.growth: 2025: approximately 2.6% annual manufacturing revenue growth, consistent with the IBISWorld 2022-2028 projected CAGR.
key_stats.broader_market_size: 2025: US adult diaper market estimated at $6.43 billion; projected 2026-2034 CAGR of 3.93%.
key_stats.demographic_driver: 2024: US population age 65+ reached 61.2 million, up 3.1% from 2023 and equal to 18.0% of the population.
key_stats.baseline_profit_margin: 2022: 18.1% EBIT margin in the IBISWorld baseline.
key_stats.baseline_employment: 2022: 5,568 employees across 11 establishments and 7 enterprises in the IBISWorld baseline.
key_stats.imports: 2022: imports were $145 million and 3.3% of domestic demand in the IBISWorld baseline; 2024 import concentration remained led by Canada, China, Mexico, Czechia and Spain according to 6Wresearch.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022: revenue increased an estimated 1.3%; 2017-2022 revenue declined at a 0.8% CAGR.
baseline_2022.profit: 2022: $790 million profit, equal to an 18.1% margin.
baseline_2022.imports: 2022: $145 million imports, equal to 3.3% of domestic demand.
baseline_2022.exports: 2022: $76 million exports, equal to 1.7% of revenue.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell branded and private-label incontinence products through drug, grocery, mass retail, e-commerce, medical supply distributors, nursing care facilities, hospitals, home-care channels and government or insurance-linked supply programs. Revenue comes from recurring consumption of disposable briefs, protective underwear, pads, underpads and premium absorbency variants, with higher margins in branded retail, specialty overnight products and direct-to-consumer subscriptions.

cost_structure.materials: 2025-2026: the largest variable costs are fluff pulp, superabsorbent polymer, polypropylene nonwovens, polyethylene film, adhesives, elastic, packaging and wetness-indicator components; US SAP prices were reported around $1,615 per metric ton in Q4 2025 and around $2.02 per kg in Q1 2026 depending on source and grade.
cost_structure.labor: 2022: wages were $483 million, or 11.1% of industry revenue; automation and high-speed converting lines keep labor below material costs.
cost_structure.profit: 2022: EBIT profit margin was 18.1%, supported by concentrated brands and the ability to pass through some input-cost inflation.
cost_structure.distribution: 2025: freight, warehousing, retail slotting, medical-distributor fees and e-commerce fulfillment remain important because products are bulky and frequently replenished.
cost_structure.capital: 2025-2026: converting equipment, absorbent-core technology, quality systems and regulatory compliance keep barriers to entry moderate to high.

major_players: Kimberly-Clark Corporation: Depend and Poise; 2025 North America segment net sales were $10.753 billion across consumer and professional categories including incontinence care.
Essity AB: TENA; 2025 Health & Medical net sales were SEK 27.468 billion and included healthcare incontinence products, while Personal Care included retail incontinence products.
First Quality Enterprises LLC: Prevail and private-label incontinence products, including protective underwear and briefs.
Attindas Hygiene Partners: adult incontinence products, including healthcare and retail channels.
Medline Industries LP: institutional incontinence products and distribution into healthcare and home-care channels.
NorthShore Care Supply: premium and specialty absorbency products, including domestically expanded MEGAMAX production in 2025.
current_dynamics: Current demand is being lifted by a larger older population, more home care, more e-commerce privacy purchasing and reduced stigma around bladder leakage. The fastest momentum is in underwear-like pull-ups, pads and discreet light-to-moderate leakage products, while tabbed briefs remain strongest in nursing homes, hospitals and severe-incontinence use cases. Input costs are less chaotic than during the 2021-2022 supply shock but remain exposed to pulp, SAP, acrylic acid, polypropylene and freight swings. Imports continue to matter at the margin, particularly from Canada, China and Mexico, but domestic production has value where retailers and healthcare channels want reliable supply, fast replenishment and quality assurance.
whats_growing: Protective underwear and pull-up formats are growing fastest because they look and feel less medical, command premium pricing and serve ambulatory consumers. Online, direct-to-consumer and subscription channels are growing because consumers value privacy and recurring delivery. Pads and liners are growing with light incontinence, female stress incontinence and younger adult use cases. Skin-health adjuncts, overnight products, extended sizing and high-absorbency specialty products are also expanding.
whats_shrinking: Traditional tabbed adult diapers are losing share in retail settings to protective underwear, although institutional demand remains stable. Lower-end undifferentiated products face pressure from private label, imports and online price comparison. Export exposure remains small, limiting growth from foreign markets. Manufacturers with older equipment or weak retail brands face margin pressure when SAP, pulp or freight costs rise.
recent_developments: 2025-06-26: The US Census Bureau reported that the 2024 population age 65+ reached 61.2 million, up 3.1% from 2023.
2025: IMARC estimated the United States adult diaper market at $6.43 billion, with a 2026-2034 CAGR forecast of 3.93%.
2025: Kimberly-Clark reported 2025 North America segment net sales of $10.753 billion across categories including Depend, Poise and other incontinence products.
2025: Essity reported 2025 Health & Medical net sales of SEK 27.468 billion, including healthcare incontinence products under TENA.
2025-05: NorthShore Care Supply expanded US manufacturing for its MEGAMAX adult diaper line across sizes XS through 3XL, according to Global Market Insights.
2026-Q1: US superabsorbent polymer prices were reported around $2.02 per kg, up from Q4 2025, reflecting firmer acrylic acid and freight costs.
outlook: The industry outlook is positive but not explosive. Manufacturing revenue is likely to grow in the low-to-mid single digits through 2026 as demographic demand, premiumization and home-care use offset import competition and mature category penetration. The clearest upside is mix: thinner, more discreet pull-ups, high-absorbency overnight products, gender-specific designs and subscription channels can lift revenue per unit even when volume growth is steady. The main risks are raw-material inflation, retailer pricing pressure, Medicaid and insurance reimbursement constraints, environmental scrutiny of disposables and further import substitution.
data_year: 2026, using latest available 2025-2026 web data and the 2022 IBISWorld baseline
one_sentence: US adult diaper manufacturers make disposable briefs, protective underwear, pads and related incontinence products for seniors, disabled consumers, home-care users and institutions, with demand rising as the 65+ population grows.

title: Adult Stores
one_liner: Adult stores remain a mature specialty retail niche where in-store advice, product trial, privacy and curated sexual-wellness assortments compete against online marketplaces and mainstream retailers.
overview: Adult Stores primarily retail sex paraphernalia and erotica through brick-and-mortar locations, including sex toys, lubricants, lingerie, BDSM accessories, enhancement products and a small remaining base of adult DVDs and magazines. The 2022 baseline defines the industry as excluding goods sold off premises through online, mail-order or phone channels, so the industry is narrower than the broader US sexual wellness market. Current 2025-2026 demand is supported by sexual wellness becoming more mainstream, but stores must differentiate through education, curated assortments, discreet service, events, premium products and omnichannel pickup because online specialists, Amazon-style marketplaces, pharmacies and big-box retailers have taken share in high-volume categories.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: approximately $16.5 billion brick-and-mortar adult-store revenue, modeled from the April 2025 IBISWorld/ResearchAndMarkets public figure of $15.8 billion in 2023 and low-single-digit 2024-2025 growth; separate public 2025 US adult-store estimates are lower at about $12.1 billion depending on definition.
key_stats.growth: 2023: +4.5% current-year growth and 2018-2023 CAGR of +7.0% in the April 2025 IBISWorld/ResearchAndMarkets synopsis; 2025-2030 growth is expected to slow as e-commerce and mainstream retailers absorb more category demand.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2022: 4.9% EBIT margin in the baseline, with 2025 margins pressured by rent, wages, card-processing, shrink, tariffs and online price transparency.
key_stats.establishments: 2022: 8,766 establishments in the baseline; 2027 baseline projection: 9,589 establishments.
key_stats.employment: 2022: 39,771 workers in the baseline; 2027 baseline projection: 43,286 workers.
key_stats.adjacent_market: 2025: US sex toys market expected to reach $11.44 billion, while the broader US sexual wellness market was estimated at $13.74 billion in 2025 and $14.82 billion in 2026 by one public forecaster.

baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: sex toys and paraphernalia accounted for more than 80.0% of revenue; vibrators were 19.2%, rubber penises 20.0%, lubrication 14.0%, anal beads 12.0%, penis rings 11.8%, rubber vaginas 8.5% and other 14.5% within the main product set.

how_it_makes_money: Stores earn revenue from in-store sales of sex toys, lubricants, condoms, lingerie, BDSM gear, novelty products, enhancement products and a declining mix of adult DVDs, magazines and other media. Higher-margin revenue comes from premium toys, branded accessories, private-label assortments, impulse add-ons, loyalty programs, events, workshops and staff-assisted upselling. Chains and franchise systems also benefit from purchasing scale, store-brand products, franchise support fees and stronger vendor terms.
cost_structure: Major costs are merchandise purchases, retail labor, rent, utilities, insurance, payment processing, local compliance, security, marketing and shrink. The 2022 baseline showed a 4.9% EBIT margin, indicating modest room to absorb price competition. In 2025, tariff exposure and the end of duty-free treatment for many China-origin low-value imports raised sourcing pressure for stores and wholesalers that depend on imported toys, lingerie and accessories.
major_players: PHE Inc. / Adam & Eve Stores
Lovers / TLA Acquisition Corp.
Lovehoney Group and its retail/wholesale brand portfolio
Spencer's / Spirit-adjacent novelty retail overlap
Local independent adult boutiques
Regional adult-store chains and franchisees
current_dynamics: The category is culturally more accepted in 2025-2026, but adult stores are no longer the only convenient point of purchase for entry-level sexual wellness products. Pharmacies, mass merchants, online marketplaces, D2C brands and app-connected device makers are expanding the addressable market while compressing store prices. Brick-and-mortar operators are responding with better lighting and merchandising, women- and couple-friendly positioning, education-led service, loyalty programs, premium body-safe products and buy-online-pickup-style convenience. Regulation remains a factor through zoning, obscenity rules, adult-content age-verification debates and state-by-state restrictions on shipping or online adult commerce.
whats_growing: 2025: premium vibrators, app-connected devices and rechargeable toys as sextech becomes more mainstream.
2025: lubricants, sexual health, pelvic-floor and menopause-adjacent products as sexual wellness is framed as health and self-care.
2025: women-focused, couple-focused, LGBTQ-inclusive and gender-neutral assortments.
2025: in-store education, workshops, loyalty programs and curated advice that online marketplaces cannot easily replicate.
2026: omnichannel models, including store locators, discreet shipping, online reservations and vendor-supported retail guides.
whats_shrinking: 2025: adult DVDs, magazines and paid physical pornography as free and subscription streaming dominate content consumption.
2025: low-end commodity toys where Amazon-style marketplaces, Temu-style import channels and big-box retailers compete on price.
2025: purely taboo or opaque store formats as consumers favor wellness-oriented, well-lit and staff-assisted retail.
2025: independent stores without purchasing scale, digital marketing capability or differentiated service.

2026: online-only adult-content traffic in states with age-verification laws, which may indirectly shift some discovery and product education back to compliant retailers but also increases privacy concerns.
recent_developments: 2025-04: IBISWorld/ResearchAndMarkets published an updated Adult Stores in the US report synopsis citing $15.8 billion of 2023 revenue and 4.5% 2023 growth.
2025-05-16: PHE Inc. filed the ADAM & EVE STORES service-mark application covering adult retail stores and franchise services.

2025-06-27: The US Supreme Court upheld Texas online adult-content age-verification requirements in Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, reinforcing a broader state regulatory trend around adult access and compliance.

2025: Grand View Research estimated the US sex toys market at $11.44 billion for 2025 and projected an 8.38% CAGR from 2025 to 2030, signaling strong product demand outside the narrow store-only definition.

2025-2026: US Customs and Border Protection guidance on China-origin imports and de minimis treatment increased landed-cost and compliance risk for retailers and distributors sourcing low-value adult products from China.
2026: Market Glass estimated the global adult-stores market at $39.1 billion in 2025, the US adult-stores market at $12.1 billion in 2025 and the global market at $48.7 billion by 2032.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive but structurally competitive. Adult stores should grow slower than the broader sexual wellness market because much of the category expansion is online or in mainstream retail. Stores with strong vendor relationships, premium assortments, staff expertise, local brand trust and discreet omnichannel options can hold share and improve basket size, while undifferentiated stores face margin pressure from e-commerce pricing, rising operating costs and tariff-sensitive imports. The most resilient operators will look less like legacy adult-video shops and more like specialty wellness retailers.
one_sentence: In 2025, US adult stores are benefiting from normalization of sex toys and sexual wellness, but growth is capped by e-commerce, mainstream retail competition, shrinking physical adult-media sales and higher import-cost pressure on China-sourced products.

title: Aerial Work Platform Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. aerial work platform manufacturers build boom lifts, scissor lifts, vertical mast lifts and related access equipment for rental fleets, contractors, infrastructure work, industrial maintenance and warehouse/logistics users.
overview: The 2022 IBISWorld baseline placed U.S. aerial work platform manufacturing revenue at $4.873 billion after a volatile 2017-2022 period shaped by the 2020 construction shock, steel-price swings and supply-chain bottlenecks. By 2025, public market data pointed to a larger U.S. aerial work platform product market of $6.85 billion, with a 2025-2030 CAGR of 6.0%, but manufacturer results were mixed: Oshkosh's Access segment and Terex's Aerials segment both reported lower 2025 sales as rental customers digested fleets and interest-sensitive projects slowed. The 2026 setup is more constructive because U.S. construction spending reached a $2.2102 trillion seasonally adjusted annual rate in May 2026 and major rental buyers are guiding to higher 2026 capital spending, but manufacturers still face tariff, customer-mix and factory-absorption pressure.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 U.S. aerial work platform market: $6.85 billion; 2030 forecast: $9.18 billion.
key_stats.growth: 2025-2030 U.S. aerial work platform market CAGR: 6.0%.
key_stats.global_market: 2025 global aerial work platform market: $11.96 billion; 2026 forecast: $12.84 billion; 2034 forecast: $24.31 billion.
key_stats.north_america_share: 2025 North America share of global aerial work platform market: 43.70%.
key_stats.construction_spending: May 2026 U.S. construction spending: $2.2102 trillion seasonally adjusted annual rate, up 0.1% from April 2026.
key_stats.rental_demand: 2026 U.S. equipment rental revenue forecast: $83.5 billion, up 3.6%.
key_stats.major_buyer_capex: United Rentals 2026 gross rental equipment purchases outlook: $4.4 billion to $4.8 billion, raised in Q1 2026.

baseline_2022.growth: 2017-2022 revenue CAGR: -4.1%; 2022 revenue growth: +8.5%; 2022-2028 projected CAGR: +1.58%.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by designing, fabricating and selling mobile elevating work platforms such as boom lifts, scissor lifts, vertical mast lifts, towable lifts and truck-mounted platforms. The largest sales channel is equipment rental companies that refresh and expand fleets; other customers include contractors, industrial facilities, utilities, aviation maintenance, agriculture, logistics and warehouse operators. Revenue is also supported by parts, attachments, telematics, safety upgrades, electric-drive variants and dealer/distributor support.
cost_structure: The largest 2025-2026 cost exposures are steel, hydraulics, engines, electric drivetrains, batteries, tires, controls, sensors, fabricated components, freight, skilled factory labor, warranty and dealer support. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline showed $981 million of wages and a 4.20% profit margin. Oshkosh's 2025 Access segment reported cost of sales of $3.6748 billion on $4.4944 billion of sales, while Terex's 2025 Aerials segment reported a 5.0% operating margin, showing how lower production volumes, discounts, tariffs and weaker factory absorption can compress margins.

current_dynamics: 2025 was a downcycle year for several OEMs even though end-user construction and rental demand remained resilient. Oshkosh Access sales fell 13.0% in 2025 and Terex Aerials sales fell 14.5% in 2025, reflecting softer market conditions, lower channel requirements, discounts and weaker demand from independent rental customers tied to smaller interest-sensitive projects. At the same time, 2026 rental-company guidance points to renewed fleet purchases: United Rentals raised its 2026 gross rental equipment purchase outlook to $4.4 billion-$4.8 billion and Herc guided to $800 million-$1.1 billion of 2026 gross rental capex. Large infrastructure, industrial, data-center, logistics and maintenance projects are offsetting weaker office and smaller private construction demand.
whats_growing: Electric-drive scissor lifts, lithium/hybrid models, telematics-enabled fleets, compact machines for aviation and warehouse work, replacement demand tied to large projects, rental-penetration-driven fleet purchases, and safety-compliant MEWP equipment aligned with ANSI/SAIA A92 standards are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: New-unit demand from smaller independent rental companies, interest-sensitive residential and light commercial projects, older diesel-only platforms in indoor or emissions-sensitive applications, and manufacturer margins exposed to tariffs, discounting and underabsorbed factory overhead shrank or weakened in 2025.
recent_developments: February 2025: JLG launched an aviation package for its ES2646 electric-drive scissor lift for aircraft manufacturing and maintenance applications.
2025: Oshkosh Access segment net sales declined 13.0% to $4.4944 billion and operating income declined 37.7% to $502.0 million.
2025: Terex Aerials net sales declined 14.5% to $2.060 billion and operating margin fell to 5.0%.
January 2026: United Rentals introduced 2026 revenue guidance of $16.8 billion-$17.3 billion and gross rental equipment purchases of $4.3 billion-$4.7 billion.
Q1 2026: United Rentals raised 2026 revenue guidance to $16.9 billion-$17.4 billion and gross rental equipment purchases to $4.4 billion-$4.8 billion.
May 2026: U.S. construction spending reached a $2.2102 trillion seasonally adjusted annual rate, up 0.1% from April 2026.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is positive but uneven. Public market forecasts put the 2025 U.S. AWP market at $6.85 billion and the 2030 market at $9.18 billion, a 6.0% CAGR, supported by rental penetration, infrastructure funding, warehouse construction, industrial maintenance and safety regulation. For manufacturers, the recovery depends on rental-fleet replacement cycles and megaproject demand converting into orders while tariffs, steel volatility, interest rates and discounting remain margin risks. The industry should grow faster than the 2022 IBISWorld baseline forecast if rental capex and large-project activity hold through 2026, but smaller-project exposure will keep revenue volatile.

Warehouse, logistics and aviation maintenance demand

title: After-School Program Providers
one_liner: US after-school providers sell supervised enrichment, tutoring, recreation and care to families, schools and public grant programs.
overview: The industry organizes youth programs outside the traditional school day in schools, community centers, clubs, parks, libraries and private learning centers. Core activities include homework help, academic enrichment, STEM, arts, sports, mentoring, meals and supervised care for working families. The 2021 baseline report put revenue at $23.4 billion in 2021 and projected slow real growth to $24.6 billion in 2026; current 2025-2026 evidence supports that mature-industry framing, with demand rising faster than funded capacity.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: $24.6 billion projected US industry revenue, in 2021 dollars, from the baseline 2021-2026 outlook.
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026: 1.0% projected annualized revenue growth in the baseline outlook.
key_stats.federal_21st_cclc: FY2025: $1.329673 billion total appropriation; FY2025: $1.309728 billion in new awards to states.
key_stats.demand: 2025: parents of nearly 30 million children wanted afterschool programs; 2025: 22.6 million children lacked access despite parent interest.
key_stats.school_access: 2024-25: 85% of US public K-12 schools offered after-school programs; 2024-25: 60% offered academically focused after-school programming; 2024-25: 42% could serve all students wanting academically focused programs.
key_stats.participation: 2024-25: public school leaders estimated 13% of public K-12 students would participate in academically focused after-school programs.
key_stats.profitability: 2021: baseline profit margin was 4.2%, reflecting labor-heavy, low-margin operations.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about $23.7 billion inferred from the baseline 2021 revenue of $23.443 billion and its 2021-2026 1.0% CAGR outlook.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: about 1.0% year-over-year implied by the baseline 2021-2026 outlook.
baseline_2022.revenue_model: 2021: tuition and service fees generated 76.3% of industry revenue.

how_it_makes_money: Providers earn revenue through parent tuition, membership fees, school-district contracts, state and local grants, federal grants such as 21st CCLC, philanthropic donations, employer-sponsored care benefits, summer and school-break fees, and add-on tutoring or enrichment charges. In 2021, the baseline file estimated tuition and service fees at 76.3% of industry revenue, making household income, parental employment and affordability central demand drivers.
cost_structure: The model is labor intensive. In 2021, wages were $15.260 billion on $23.443 billion of baseline revenue, or about 65.1% of revenue. Remaining costs include rent or school-space charges, insurance, transportation, food and snacks, curriculum materials, licensing and background checks, technology, administration, marketing and compliance. Profitability is thin: the baseline file estimated a 2021 margin of 4.2%.
major_players: Boys & Girls Clubs of America: 2024 data reported more than 4 million young people served annually and more than 5,500 Club locations.
YMCA of the USA and local YMCAs: major nonprofit provider of youth development, childcare, camp and after-school programming, with 2025 audited financial disclosure available from YMCA of the USA.

KinderCare Champions: 2025 expansion added more than 200 new before- and after-school sites for the 2025-26 school year, adding more than 10,000 new child-care spots and entering Connecticut, Minnesota and New Mexico.
Kumon: 2024-25 annual report showed 1,197,493 enrollments outside Japan in December 2024 across 8,384 centers, relevant to the tutoring and academic-enrichment side of the market.
4-H, school districts, local parks and recreation departments, faith-based nonprofits and community-based organizations: the industry remains highly fragmented with many local operators.
current_dynamics: Demand is high but capacity is constrained. In 2025, Afterschool Alliance found parents of nearly 30 million children wanted afterschool programs, but 22.6 million children were not accessing them. Public funding remains crucial: FY2025 21st CCLC appropriations were $1.329673 billion, while 2024-25 NCES data showed 47% of schools with academically focused after-school programs used federal grants or other federal programs. Operators are balancing full enrollment, waitlists, higher wage expectations, transportation gaps and the end of pandemic-era ESSER support after the September 30, 2024 obligation deadline.
whats_growing: Academic recovery, STEM, tutoring, mental-health and social-emotional supports, summer learning, school-district partnerships, employer-supported childcare benefits and private operators with school-site contracts are growing. Demand from working parents is strong: in 2025, 82% of parents with a child in an afterschool program said it helped them keep their job, and 92% said they were less stressed knowing their child was safe.
whats_shrinking: Unsubsidized access for low- and middle-income families is under pressure as 2025 cost barriers persist. ESSER-funded expansions are shrinking after the 2024 federal deadline, and some providers are reducing hours, staffing or slots where grants do not replace pandemic aid. Purely fee-based programs serving price-sensitive households face weaker growth than subsidized or contract-backed programs.
recent_developments: 2024-09-30: ARP ESSER obligation period ended, forcing FY2025 sustainability planning for after-school and summer learning programs.
2024-11-14: NCES reported 85% of US public K-12 schools offered after-school programs for 2024-25, but only 42% could serve all interested students in academically focused programs.
2025-07-16: OMB released Title IV-B 21st CCLC funds after a 2025 federal funding freeze, according to AASA reporting.
2025-08-26: KinderCare Champions announced more than 200 new site wins for the 2025-26 school year and more than 10,000 new child-care spots.
2025-10-15: Afterschool Alliance released America After 3PM 2025, finding 22.6 million children lacked access despite parent interest.
2026-04-02: Afterschool Alliance reported 88% of providers were concerned about long-term funding and program future based on a late-2025 provider survey.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modest real revenue growth with strong underlying demand but limited funded capacity. The baseline projection of $24.6 billion in 2026 remains a reasonable anchor, but the mix is shifting toward providers that can secure district contracts, 21st CCLC subgrants, state expanded-learning funds and philanthropic support. Upside comes from unmet demand, working-parent needs, academic recovery and youth well-being concerns; downside comes from wage inflation, transportation limits, federal funding uncertainty and affordability barriers.
one_sentence: After-school program providers remain a fragmented, low-margin care and enrichment industry with strong 2025 family demand, constrained access, staffing pressure and heavy exposure to public funding decisions.

title: Air & Gas Compressor Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. air and gas compressor makers sell mature but mission-critical equipment into factories, energy, utilities, construction and process industries, with demand pulled between industrial activity, energy production and import competition.
overview: Air and gas compressor manufacturers produce air compressors, industrial and specialty gas compressors, vacuum pumps, industrial spraying equipment and related parts. The equipment is embedded in manufacturing lines, oil and gas production and transmission, utilities, mining, construction rental fleets, food and pharma plants, and semiconductor or electronics production. The baseline IBISWorld file put 2022 revenue at $10.304 billion after a 2020 shock and a partial 2021-2022 recovery; a 2025 industry snapshot citing IBISWorld placed 2025 U.S. revenue at $9.8 billion, implying the sector has not fully regained the baseline. Current conditions are mixed: U.S. industrial production was 1.7% above year-earlier levels in May 2026 and energy production set records in 2025, but import penetration, higher steel and aluminum tariffs, and still-below-average manufacturing capacity utilization keep margins and volumes under pressure.

key_stats.growth: 2022-2025 implied revenue CAGR of approximately -1.7%, based on $10.304 billion in 2022 and $9.8 billion in 2025

how_it_makes_money.business_model: Manufacturers earn revenue from new compressor systems, engineered packages, vacuum systems, portable and stationary compressors, parts, fluids, controls, installation support and lifecycle service. Large customers buy on reliability, uptime, energy efficiency, pressure and flow specifications, service coverage and compliance rather than price alone.
customer_markets: oil and gas extraction and processing

cost_structure.materials_and_components: High share of cost from steel, aluminum, castings, motors, valves, rotors, controls, electronics and bought-in components; 2025 Section 232 tariff changes increased exposure for steel and aluminum content.
cost_structure.labor: 2022 wages were $1.671 billion, about 16.2% of industry revenue; 2026 machinery manufacturing hourly earnings were near $39 for all employees and about $31 for production and nonsupervisory employees.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 EBIT margin was 5.2%, below many branded industrial equipment peers because of cyclicality, input costs, trade exposure and competition.
cost_structure.service_and_aftermarket: Parts, fluids, repair and maintenance carry more stable demand and typically better resilience during capex slowdowns than new unit sales.
cost_structure.trade_exposure: Imports are a structural cost and pricing constraint; 2024 HS 841480 imports alone were $3.906 billion, with Mexico the largest source.

current_dynamics: The market is balancing better end-market pull from energy, process industries and infrastructure against weak-to-mixed general manufacturing and higher input-cost volatility. Record 2025 U.S. natural gas and crude oil production supports demand for gas compression, vapor recovery, air systems and maintenance parts. Factory demand is less uniform: Federal Reserve data show May 2026 manufacturing output was flat month over month and manufacturing utilization at 75.7%, below its long-run average, so replacement and efficiency projects matter more than broad capacity expansion. Trade policy is a new pressure point because 2025 steel and aluminum tariff changes expanded derivative coverage to compressors and pumps, affecting imported components and finished equipment while also raising potential pricing power for domestic production.
whats_growing: Oil-free compressors for food, pharma, electronics and other regulated environments
Variable-speed-drive and high-efficiency systems that reduce electricity consumption
Electric portable compressors for rental, construction and indoor or low-emission jobsites
Aftermarket parts, fluids, remanufacturing and predictive maintenance services
Gas compression linked to LNG exports, shale gas, gathering, processing and pipeline takeaway capacity
Smart compressors with connected monitoring, controls and maintenance analytics
whats_shrinking: Low-margin commodity compressor lines exposed to Mexican, Chinese and other imported alternatives
Purely diesel-driven portable compressor demand where electric jobsite equipment is feasible
New-unit purchases by customers delaying capital expenditures in soft manufacturing segments
Export competitiveness when the U.S. dollar is strong or when retaliatory trade measures hit machinery
Standalone products without service contracts, controls or energy-efficiency differentiation
recent_developments: 2025-04: IBISWorld published a 2025 U.S. Air & Gas Compressor Manufacturing industry update through market research distributors.
2025-06: The White House increased Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs to 50% effective June 4, 2025, raising input-cost and landed-cost exposure for machinery.
2025-08: Commerce added 407 derivative steel and aluminum product categories, explicitly including compressors and pumps, to Section 232 tariff coverage.
2025-08: A distributor industry update citing IBISWorld placed 2025 U.S. sector revenue at $9.8 billion.
2026-03: EIA reported U.S. marketed natural gas production reached a 2025 record of 118.5 Bcf/d, supporting gas compression demand.
2026-06: Federal Reserve data showed May 2026 industrial production up 1.7% year over year but manufacturing utilization still only 75.7%.
outlook: Through 2026, the industry should grow modestly from the 2025 trough but remain cyclical. Upside comes from oil and gas production, LNG export infrastructure, utilities work, factory automation, energy-efficient replacements and aftermarket service. The main constraints are import competition, high materials sensitivity, tariff pass-through risk, soft capex in weaker manufacturing niches and the maturity of the installed base. A realistic near-term view is low-single-digit nominal revenue growth, with better margins for branded OEMs that bundle service, controls, energy savings and specialized oil-free or gas-compression solutions.
one_sentence: The industry is a mature machinery niche whose 2025 revenue is below the 2022 baseline, but 2026 demand is being supported by record U.S. oil and gas output, steadier industrial production, aftermarket parts and efficiency-focused compressor upgrades.
